Actor-specific slopes require directed or bipartite data and unit-spaced periods.

keep_per_actor

one of "auto" (default; full draws when memory cost < 250 MB else streaming summary), "draws" (full [n_iter, n_actors, T] cube), "summary" (streaming posterior mean + sd only), or "none" (only hyperparameter chains).

time_index

optional numeric vector of length \(T\) giving observation times. Default NULL treats periods as equally spaced. Strictly-increasing values are required when supplied. Unequal gaps scale the AR(1) / RW1 transition variance and are also used by the RW2 and Matern 3/2 dynamic-beta precision builders.

period_exposure

optional non-negative numeric vector of length \(T\) giving period-level exposure offsets. Wired for Poisson: when supplied with any value != 1, the Poisson observation likelihood becomes \(Y_{ij,t} \sim \text{Poisson}(e_t \cdot \exp(Z_{ij,t}))\), while the latent \(Z\) retains its existing semantic of "unexposed log-rate". For other families, non-trivial period_exposure is an error (rescale Y or use a covariate offset). NULL (default) or all-ones uses the unscaled likelihood path. Zero exposure is supported when all observed counts in that period are zero; its observed log-likelihood is zero.

max_seconds

optional positive scalar; if the MCMC wall-clock time exceeds this many seconds, the chain terminates cleanly and fit$terminated_early is set to TRUE. The draw arrays hold the draws stored until then. When the time runs out before the first stored draw, fit$no_draws_stored is TRUE, every draw array (BETA, VC and the others) has no draws along its draw dimension, the posterior means are NA, print() says so, and coef(), summary() and the other methods that summarise draws stop with an error of class lame_no_draws; lame_resume(fit, nscan_more = N, max_seconds = Inf) continues the chains.

checkpoint_path

optional file path. When set, the chain periodically writes BETA, VC, the full sampler state, seed, completed iteration count, remaining burn-in and original call to this file. Use lame_resume or pass the same path back as resume_from = path to continue.

checkpoint_every

positive integer; iterations between checkpoint writes. Default 100L.

log_lik_method

one of "observed_exact" (default), "observed_ghk", or "augmented". Observed marginal scores are supported for normal, binary, Poisson-lognormal and explicit-cutpoint ordinal fits. Poisson integration uses an adaptive log-integral with concavity bounds on omitted tails. Capped nominations, fixed ranks and data-induced ordinal models do not have the cellwise observed likelihood claimed by "observed_exact"; such requests fail explicitly. The existing "observed_ghk" rank estimators are approximate diagnostics, and "augmented" stores Gaussian-on-Z latent diagnostics; loo() and waic() refuse both with an error of class "lame_loo_factorization_unsupported", and read_log_lik() returns the scores. Even correct cell marginal scores require independent residual cells, or unique unordered dyads in symmetric fits, before LOO or WAIC can use them. Directed correlated cell marginals require joint dyad factors, which are not supplied by this interface. Inspect fit$log_lik_contract. "augmented" uses the augmented-data Gaussian-on-\(Z\) contribution. Note the GHK cost grows exponentially with the per-row dimension \(D\) (the number of observed dyads in a sender row): the per-row Monte Carlo budget escalates to min(2048, max(64, 8 * 2^D)) draws across a bank of 8 randomized Halton sequences, once per stored draw, so "observed_ghk" on a unipartite "frn" fit with more than roughly 12 actors (where \(D = n - 1\)) is expensive; rows with \(D > 15\) fall back to a fast pairwise-normal approximation. Power users can fix the per-row budget exactly via prior$ghk_n_mc (a single positive integer), which both raises the 2048 ceiling and lowers the 8 * 2^D accuracy floor; lower budgets increase the downward Jensen bias of the log-lik estimate.

ordinal_cutpoints

character: cutpoint convention for family = "ordinal". "data_induced" (default) uses the data-induced cutpoints; "explicit" samples ordered cutpoints with the first fixed at zero and unit latent residual variance. Independent directed and symmetric models use the Cowles (1996) marginal Metropolis-Hastings update. Directed models with dcor = TRUE use cutpoint Gibbs updates conditional on the correlated latent observations. Explicit cutpoints are supported for unipartite models; predictions retain the original numeric category labels and use each saved cutpoint draw. Ignored for other families.

method

character: "mcmc" (default, the Bayesian MCMC fit) or "als" (the fast, MCMC-free empirical-Bayes fit, which reports a standard error for every estimate). With no dynamic arguments, method = "als" uses the pooled-static lame_als estimator. Both methods return named actors sorted by name. For normal, binary, and Poisson panels, method = "als" also supports a dynamic empirical-Bayes estimator (see the section Dynamic fast fits) for dynamic_ab, selected dynamic_beta, smooth AR(1) dynamic_uv in directed, symmetric, and bipartite panels, and Student-t dynamic_uv in directed and symmetric panels (bipartite t requests are refused). dynamic_uv_kind = "snap" is refused on this route (use method = "mcmc"). On the dynamic route rho_ab, sigma_ab, rho_uv, sigma_uv, rho_beta and sigma_beta are set under the hyperpriors of lame() (the variance components and persistences by EM, the stationary variance of moving positions by a profile of the marginal objective). The fit can seed a warm-started MCMC run via als_start_vals. Under dynamic_ab the reported VC entries va and vb are the variances of the actor levels, as in an MCMC fit, estimated by EM (fit$eb$sab). Node-covariate coefficients use the same orthogonal additive-effect decomposition as lame_als; dynamic node coefficients use period-specific node values when selected by dynamic_beta, while static node coefficients use per-actor means. Named changing-composition panels are aligned to the union actor set; the fit treats an absent actor-period as a free AR state. Posterior draws and rank/censored families are not handled by the ALS routes. Dynamic ALS prediction evaluates the fitted periods, optionally with replacement dyadic covariates; predict(fit, h = ...) forecasting is not implemented and a positive horizon is refused. With method = "als", a binary network whose observed density \(d\) has \(\min(d, 1 - d) < 0.20\) (ties among the observed cells, the diagonal of a one-mode network left out, pooled over periods) is fitted with a warning: there the sampler is the better choice.

als_stability

character (only used when method = "als" and a dynamic ALS path is selected): "none" (default), "quick", or "validation". The non-"none" presets rerun the dynamic ALS fit from jittered starts and attach fit$stability, which reports fitted-surface and coefficient-path differences across starts.

als_max_iter

positive integer (only used when method = "als"): maximum iterations for the selected ALS solver. Default 1000. The dynamic empirical-Bayes estimator needs up to a few hundred passes on a weakly identified panel; the Gaussian-transition fit of a 40 x 10 panel takes about 150 passes at the scale its search settles on. A dynamic fit that has not met its convergence criterion in this many iterations is an error of class "lame_als_convergence"; its field fit holds the last iterate. A static fit that does not converge is refused in the same way, without a fit field (see max_iter in ame_als).

als_tol

optional positive scalar (only used when method = "als"): convergence tolerance for the ALS objective and fitted values. NULL keeps each ALS estimator's built-in default. The dynamic empirical-Bayes estimator stops when every block's scaled score is below sqrt(als_tol) and, for moving positions, the objective has settled to within als_tol deviance units of the fixed point; for a Poisson fit the estimated distance of the noise variance ve to the limit of its iteration must be below the threshold as well.

als_lowrank_method

optional character: inner solver for the low-rank factor block of the dynamic fast fit that seeds the warm start of a dynamic_uv chain (see Details), "mm", "als", or "hybrid". NULL (default) keeps "hybrid". With method = "als" the dynamic empirical-Bayes estimator solves the factors jointly with the other effects by Gauss-Newton and warns that the argument does not apply; the static fast route (no dynamic arguments) does not use it.

als_linear_solver

optional character (only used when method = "als" with no dynamic arguments): linear solver for the static block updates, "eigen", "qr", or "auto". NULL (default) keeps lame_als's default ("eigen"). The dynamic ALS route uses its own path solvers and aborts if a value is given.

als_multistart

optional character (only used when method = "als" with no dynamic arguments, and R > 0): "none", "cheap", or "full", forwarded to lame_als. NULL (default) defers to multistart. Supplying both uses als_multistart.

multistart

character (only used when method = "als" with no dynamic arguments, and R > 0): "none" (default), "cheap" (4 starts), or "full" (8 starts). Forwarded to lame_als, which reruns the block-coordinate fit from several starts and keeps the one with the lowest objective. The dynamic ALS route has no multi-start and ignores this argument with a warning; use als_stability there instead.

bootstrap

integer (only used when method = "als"): number of bootstrap replicates. 0 (default) skips the bootstrap: every fit already carries analytic standard errors. N >= 30 runs N replicates of a static fit and attaches the result, so that vcov(), confint and summary() report the bootstrap errors of the coefficients, with the analytic error kept for any quantity the bootstrap gives none (a smaller positive N is an error, raised before anything is fitted). Each replicate is drawn as ame_als_bootstrap draws it and refit from the fitted state; a replicate that has not converged within als_max_iter iterations is retried at four times that budget and otherwise dropped, never kept. A bootstrap that cannot run on the fitted model (more than 5 percent of the replicates dropped, for example), and any bootstrap of a dynamic fit, whose empirical-Bayes standard errors are its own, leaves the fit with its analytic standard errors and a message of class "lame_als_bootstrap_not_run".

bootstrap_type

character (only used when method = "als"): "parametric" (default) or "block". The block scheme needs at least ten resampling blocks (ceiling(T / bootstrap_block_length)); on a shorter panel it runs the parametric scheme instead, with a message. The block scheme gives no replicate standard error for the parameters that resampling time slices cannot vary (see ame_als_bootstrap); they keep their analytic errors.

bootstrap_block_length

integer: block length for the block bootstrap.

bootstrap_seed

optional integer seed for the bootstrap.

chains

integer: the number of independently seeded chains (default 2, or getOption("lame.chains")). Chain \(k\) runs with seed seed + 1000 * (k - 1). With chains > 1 the chains are checked, compared and pooled (see the convergence policy); chains = 1 runs one chain and the drift check only. ALS fits run one chain.

cores

integer or NULL: workers for the chains. The chains run forked on Unix, at most one worker per chain; NULL uses getOption("lame.cores") if set and otherwise all cores but one. Windows runs the chains one after the other.

resume_from

optional path to a checkpoint file produced by a previous lame(..., checkpoint_path = path) call. When non-NULL, lame() short-circuits all other input parsing and delegates to lame_resume with the user-supplied overrides forwarded. Pass nscan = K to request K additional post-burn sweeps on the continuation. Supply checkpoint_path and max_seconds again to checkpoint or limit the continuation. Unfinished burn-in is completed before any new posterior draws are stored. Default NULL.

sampler

MCMC transition method. Default "gibbs" retains the established sampler. "tempered" uses exact observed-probit replica exchange for symmetric binary networks with positive static rank, a random-walk intercept and optional symmetric dyadic covariates, and shared dynamic additive effects on a common actor grid. Its default burn-in is 15,000 sweeps and default post-burn length is 200,000 sweeps. See Details for its explicit latent-coordinate prior and supported options.

Value

auto_extend

the record of the convergence policy: max_extensions, extensions (made), discarded_sweeps, triggers (a list with the flagged quantities of each extension) and the thresholds used.

BETA

posterior samples of regression coefficients. A 2-dimensional matrix [n_stored, p] when all coefficients are static. When dynamic_beta flags any coefficient as time-varying, BETA is a 3-dimensional array [n_stored, p, T] whose third dimension is the time period. Static coefficients are still present with their values replicated across the third dimension. coef(fit) collapses this to a [p, T] posterior-mean matrix.

Migration from amen. Under amen::ame() the BETA slot was always 2-D. Scripts that compute apply(fit$BETA, 2, mean) on an amen fit will silently aggregate across periods when run against a lame() fit with dynamic_beta active (the second margin is the coefficient index in both shapes; the new third margin is time). Use length(dim(fit$BETA)) to detect the shape, or call coef(fit) which returns a [p, T] matrix in either case.

VC

posterior samples of the variance parameters. On a unipartite directed binary panel of two periods or more carrying fewer than 1.2 events per actor-period, the draws of va and vb are kept here but summary(), print() and confint() report them as not estimated, with the measured coverage. Under a supplied effects prior the variance draws are reported under it (see prior_supplied)

events_per_actor_period

for the families with an event rate (binary, cbin, frn, poisson) on a panel of at least two periods, the mean over periods of the events per row actor; the rate the reporting methods read

events_per_actor

on the same panels, the events per row actor over the whole panel (every period's events over the actors present in any period), quoted with the rate

prior_supplied

TRUE when prior carried Sab0, eta0 or etaab: where the data alone leave the effect variances to the prior (the sparse rule, a saturated cap) the reporting methods then show them under the supplied prior; the intercept and row-covariate coefficients a saturated cap withholds stay withheld

odmax_saturated_share

for the cbin and frn families, the share of observed rows whose observed outdegree sits at their odmax; the reporting methods read it alongside events_per_actor_period and stop reporting va, cab, the intercept and any row-covariate coefficient at 80 percent or above (60 percent for a panel of one period; odmax_sat_threshold records the one applied) (vb stays reported; see odmax)

APM

posterior mean of additive row effects a

BPM

posterior mean of additive column effects b

APM_sd, BPM_sd

posterior standard deviation of each additive effect (static effects), used by simulate() to draw the effects

U

multiplicative row effects u. For static positions, a matrix (n x R) that factors the posterior mean product at rank R, columns in decreasing order of its singular values. For dynamic_uv = TRUE, a 3D array (n x R x T) whose periods factor the posterior mean product of each period at rank R and are aligned across periods; NA for an actor absent from a period (see latent_positions)

V

multiplicative column effects v (asymmetric case), with the same layout as U

U_sd, V_sd

for static positions with saved latent draws (posterior_options(save_UV = TRUE)), and for dynamic_uv = TRUE with saved latent draws (the default), the posterior standard deviation of each reported coordinate, each draw matched onto the reported positions by a move that leaves its product unchanged, same shape as U and V; latent_positions() reports them as posterior_sd. A method = "als" fit with static factors (dynamic_ab or dynamic_beta without dynamic_uv) reports the Laplace sd of each reported coordinate, with the directions that leave the product unchanged left out (below the signal threshold at least the variational sd of each row, as ame_als()), and an undirected one also L_sd and L_ci, the sd and interval of each eigenvalue

UVPM

on the union of actors; under changing composition the dynamic array has NA rows and columns for actors absent from a period, and a static fit gives one matrix for every pair. posterior mean of UV

ULUPM

posterior mean of ULU (symmetric case)

L

for symmetric fits, the diagonal of the product \(U L U'\): the eigenvalues of ULUPM when the positions are static; when they are dynamic, one diagonal for every period that carries the scale and sign of each direction, so that \(U_t L U_t'\) is the best rank-R part of each period's ULUPM with those signs

EZ

posterior mean of the linear predictor Z, on the link scale for every family (the log rate for Poisson, the probit scale for the binary, ordinal, cbin and frn families); YPM is the response-scale counterpart. For mode = "bipartite", EZ is a list of per-period matrices with the row and column actors as dimnames, in the lexicographic sort of the input actor names (so "r10" sorts before "r2" unless you zero-pad).

YPM

Stored response-scale fitted value, one matrix per period: the average over the stored draws of the mean response given each draw, which is the tie probability for binary fits, the linear predictor for normal fits and the expected category value for ordinal fits with explicit cutpoints. For cbin, frn and data-induced ordinal fits it is the average of ten outcomes replicated at each stored draw. For Poisson fits it is the mean count \(e_t \exp(\eta + \sigma^2 / 2)\) at the posterior means of the linear predictor and of the residual variance; see the Poisson model details.

coefficient_prior

Recorded specification of the coefficient prior used by the fitting build, as displayed by prior_summary().

static_uv_prior

For static asymmetric unipartite factors, the inverse-Wishart covariance prior's degrees of freedom, scale and dimension, the data scale \(s\) of Suv0 = s I (data_scale) and the multiplier of \(2R + 2\) in the degrees of freedom (df_multiplier; see kappa0 in ame). Older fit objects do not carry this record.

sampler_health

A data frame separating numerical failures from valid prior-bound rejections for each conditional sampler step. The compatibility counts in tryErrorChecks and mh_counters contain both. A numerical failure, in a conditional step or in a joint Hamiltonian, actor-factor slice or bipartite scale move, aborts the fit with an error of class lame_sampler_failure (the counts are in the health field of the condition), so a returned fit has none. A proposal outside the prior's box (prior$uv_max_abs, prior$G_max) is a Metropolis rejection of the model, counted here; summary() states it when it is on one percent or more of the sweeps. Joint Hamiltonian acceptance and rejection records are kept in their corresponding move fields. sampler_health_iterations gives the number of sweeps counted, including burn-in.

exact_fallbacks

Named counts of the times a step kept its state after a numerical failure where keeping it leaves the posterior invariant (a block skipped given quantities it does not move, a proposal rejected, or the same conditional drawn by a second kernel). They do not stop the fit; print() and summary() state them, and a count above a tenth of the sweeps warns with class lame_exact_fallbacks. Empty when there was none.

var_cap_hits

number of sweeps in which a stationary-variance cap (prior$uv_var_cap, prior$ab_var_cap) removed most of a conditional draw

level_move

for binary unipartite and bipartite fits, the attempts, accepts, acceptance rate and final step SD of the level direction of the joint scale move (absent when the move did not run)

actor_move

for Poisson and ordinal fits, the work of the translations: visits, the level translations drawn (level_calls) with the likelihood evaluations of the Poisson ones (level_evals) and the steps that failed to terminate (stuck) or that were left to the sampler because the current state lay outside the interval the translation needs (skipped), the draws of the location of the latent array (location_calls, ordinal), the coefficient translations (coef_calls, coef_evals, coef_stuck; Poisson), the position steps (uv_calls, uv_evals, uv_stuck; Poisson with static positions) and the attempts and accepts of the scale move of the dyadic variance and correlation (scale_attempts, scale_accepts, and rho_attempts, rho_accepts of its correlation-only proposals; Poisson: the carried scale move, with dynamic_rho the one of the translations); for binary fits, the work of the collapsed per-actor update: visits, the slice steps of the level translations (level_calls) and of the static positions (uv_calls), the likelihood evaluations they used (level_evals, uv_evals), the steps that failed to terminate (stuck) and the attempts and accepts of the reciprocity update (rho_attempts, rho_accepts; zero for bipartite fits, which add the slice steps of the deviation paths of actor pairs under dynamic_ab, dev_calls and dev_evals); for "cbin" and "frn" fits, the work of the receiver-level translation: visits, the receivers moved (col_calls) and the receivers left to the sampler because the current state lay outside the interval the translation needs (col_skips), the sweeps in which the level update moved a set of rows (level_calls) and the rows it moved (level_rows), the sweeps in which the period update translated a set of periods (period_calls) and the sets it moved (period_comps), the proposals and accepts of the collapsed translation of the periods that have rows with room (room_attempts, room_accepts) and the moves refused because a redraw did not terminate (room_stuck), and the proposals and accepts of the reciprocity update (rho_attempts, rho_accepts); with moving positions, Poisson and binary fits add the path steps drawn (dpm_calls), the likelihood evaluations they used (dpm_evals) and those that failed to terminate (dpm_stuck), and symmetric fits the proposals and accepts of the scale ridge draw (dpm_scale_attempts, dpm_scale_accepts); absent when the updates did not run

beta_hyper_move

for dynamic_beta fits, the sweeps, proposals and accepts of the interweaving step of the path hyperparameters and its acceptance rate; absent when the step did not run

poisson_period_move

for "poisson" fits, the visits, the translations of the periods (period_calls) and of the whole paths (path_calls) and of the static coefficients (static_calls) drawn, the evaluations their slice steps used, and the proposals and accepts of the carried scale move (scale_attempts, scale_accepts, and for the correlation alone scale_rho_attempts, scale_rho_accepts); absent when the moves did not run

binary_scale_move

for "binary" fits, the draws of the scale of the linear predictor (visits), the evaluations of its density they used (evals) and the draws that moved the state (moved); absent when the draw did not run

ordinal_scale_move

for "ordinal" fits, the sweeps the scale moves visited (visits) and the sweeps at which the scale of the whole state moved (orbit_moved); absent when the moves did not run

pa_hyper_move

for dynamic_beta_per_actor fits, the sweeps, proposals and accepts of the interweaving step of the actor-specific slope hyperparameters and its acceptance rate; absent when the step did not run

uv_nc_move

for dynamic_uv fits of the "ar1" and "snap" kinds, the calls and the draws that changed the value (sym_calls, sym_moved, bip_calls, bip_moved) of the non-centred persistence step (symmetric) and scale step (bipartite); absent when the move did not run

uv_nc_hyper_move

for directed and bipartite dynamic_uv fits of the "ar1" kind under the stationary-variance prior (prior$uv_var_shape), the visits and the accepted proposals of the non-centred update of rho_uv and the stationary variance (four proposals of each per visit, and four more of each with the latent array carried along in binary and Poisson fits); absent when the step did not run

uv_temper_move

for symmetric Poisson dynamic_uv fits, the tempered transitions made, accepted and those that changed the sign of the weight; absent when the move did not run

ab_period_move

for "poisson" fits with dynamic_ab, the sweeps, the pairs (or single effects) moved and the slice evaluations of the translations of the actor-period effects; absent when the move did not run

ab_hyper_move

for dynamic_ab fits, the proposals and accepts of the update of the additive-effect hyperparameters given the totals and the acceptance rate; absent when the update did not run

uv_g_scale_move

for bipartite fits with static positions, the number of sweeps and of rescaled coordinates of the draw along the scale ridge of the positions and the interaction matrix; absent when the update did not run

marginal_move

For supported binary fits, joint-update attempts, accepts, acceptance rate, final step size and numerical rejections.

bipartite_scale_move

For supported Gaussian, binary, Poisson or ordinal bipartite fits, joint scale attempts, accepts, acceptance rate, prior-bound rejections and numerical rejections. The fixed proposal requires no adaptive tuning.

actor_factor_slice

For supported binary fits, completed paired actor/factor rounds, block and likelihood evaluation counts, prior-bound rejections, and separate numerical failures.

dynamic_marginal_move

For supported binary fits with moving factors, Hamiltonian attempts, accepts, acceptance rate, tuned step size, numerical rejections, prior-bound rejections and proposals whose likelihood underflowed to zero density (underflow_rejections).

nc_ar_move

Attempts and accepts for the joint persistence and path-scale updates of the factors and actor effects.

translation_move

Number of visits to the factor/actor translation update, counting each margin separately.

rho_collapsed_move

Attempts, accepts and acceptance rate for dyadic correlation updates with binary latent responses integrated out.

uv_scale_move

Attempts, accepts and acceptance rate for joint latent-factor and innovation-scale updates.

dev_move

the same for the deviation direction, present for binary unipartite dynamic_ab fits

als_start

for dynamic_uv fits, whether the chain started from a dynamic ALS fit (FALSE when start values were supplied, when prior$als_start = FALSE, for the snap kind, symmetric and bipartite fits and the rank families, or when the ALS fit failed or fell outside the range the sampler holds)

sigma_ab_prior_scale

for dynamic_ab fits, the inverse-gamma scale of the deviation innovation variance, fixed before sampling

sigma_beta_prior_scale

for dynamic_beta fits, the inverse-gamma scale of the coefficient innovation variance, fixed before sampling from the response scale

G

for bipartite fits, the interaction matrix of \(U G V'\): the identity when the positions are static (the scale is split evenly between U and V, and \(U G V'\) is the best rank-R part of UVPM); when they are dynamic, a diagonal matrix fixed across periods that carries the scale, so that \(U_t G V_t'\) is the best rank-R part of each period's UVPM

GOF

a named list with one element per goodness-of-fit statistic (sd.rowmean, sd.colmean, dyad.dep, cycle.dep, trans.dep; for mode = "bipartite", sd.rowmean, sd.colmean, four.cycles, with four.cycle.dep replacing the count for Gaussian outcomes). Weighted rectangle dependence is NA when no complete rectangle is observed or the values have zero variance; see gof_stats_bipartite. Each element is a [T, 1 + n_stored] matrix: one row per period, the first column the observed value and the rest the posterior predictive draws. For the data-induced ordinal family the predictive draws are quantile-matched to observed category frequencies and assess dependence conditional on those frequencies. Explicit ordinal fits instead use each draw's sampled cutpoints, allowing checks of category frequencies as well. See gof for post-hoc computation and gof_plot for visualization.

a_level, b_level

for dynamic_ab = TRUE, the posterior means of the per-actor levels behind the effect paths; predict() and simulate() propagate the deviation around them

a_dynamic, b_dynamic

for dynamic_ab = TRUE, the posterior mean effect paths (actors by periods), with a_dynamic_sd / b_dynamic_sd their posterior sds

rho_ab, sigma_ab, rho_uv, sigma_uv

draws of the AR(1) persistence and innovation scale of the dynamic effects and positions, when fitted

start_vals

Final parameter values from MCMC, can be used as the input for a future model run.

model.name

Name of the model (if provided)

Details

This command provides posterior inference for parameters in AME models of longitudinal relational data, assuming one of six possible data types/models. The model supports both unipartite networks (square adjacency matrices) and bipartite networks (rectangular adjacency matrices with distinct row and column node sets) across multiple time points.

Tempered symmetric binary sampling:

Set sampler = "tempered" for a common actor grid with family = "binary", symmetric = TRUE, dynamic_ab = TRUE, positive static rank, an intercept and optional symmetric dyadic covariates. At least four actors and two equally spaced periods are required. The observed likelihood contains each unordered dyad once: $$P(Y_{ijt}=1)=\Phi(x_{ijt}^{T}\beta+\mu_t+a_{it}+a_{jt}+u_i^T\Lambda u_j).$$ As on the other routes the intercept moves under dynamic_ab, with the kind dynamic_beta_kind gives it ("rw1" when that is "ar1"). The intercept of period \(t\) is the intercept coefficient plus \(\mu_t\), with \(\mu_1=0\); for "rw1" \(\mu_t-\mu_{t-1}\sim N(0,\sigma_\beta^2\lambda_0)\); for "rw2" the second differences have that distribution and the first increment does too; for "matern32" \(\mu_t\) is the change since the first period of a Matern 3/2 process with variance \(\sigma_\beta^2\lambda_0\) and length scale prior$matern32_length_scale (default \(\max(2, T/4)\) periods). \(\sigma_\beta^2\) is inverse-gamma with shape prior$sigma_beta_shape and scale prior$sigma_beta_scale and \(\lambda_0\) is the innovation scale of the intercept; BETA holds the intercept per period. Shared actor effects comprise a zero-sum level and a zero-sum stationary Gaussian AR(1) deviation. Their level variance has an inverse-gamma prior with shape etaab/2 and scale etaab * Sab0[1,1]/2; the innovation variance has shape sigma_ab_shape and scale sigma_ab_scale. Persistence has its specified normal prior truncated to \((-0.99,0.99)\). Coefficients retain the panel-design Gaussian prior.

prior$uv_prior = "hierarchical" retains the static symmetric factor prior: signed weights are independent standard normals, and each raw coordinate column has variance \(v_k\sim IG(1,0.5)\). This is the default for the tempered sampler. The explicitly selected alternative prior$uv_prior = "unit" fixes every coordinate variance at one; it changes the model's prior, not just its sampling algorithm. Raw factors are centered for reporting, with compensating actor-level and intercept shifts that preserve every joint predictor.

The sampler uses bounded Langevin proposals with their complete forward and reverse Gaussian densities, a fixed ladder of 21 likelihood powers, replica exchanges, prior refreshes at power zero, and signed-weight reflections. After each Langevin step every replica redraws its scale parameters given the centred effects (an interweaving step, Yu and Meng 2011): the level variance from its inverse-gamma conditional given the levels, \((\rho_{ab}, \sigma_{ab})\) jointly given the deviation paths (a slice update of the persistence with the innovation variance integrated out, then the innovation variance), and \(\sigma_\beta\) given the intercept path; the latent effects and every linear predictor are unchanged by this step. It then updates the intercept of each period on its own, by a random-walk Metropolis step that leaves the other periods' intercepts in place. Under the non-centred coordinates of the Langevin step alone these scales and the first-period intercept move as a slow random walk. The replica at power one, whose states are stored, makes four such transitions per sweep and every other replica one. Step sizes adapt only during burn-in. fit$tempering records transition counts, step sizes and replica sign traces, one record per chain in a fit of several chains.

The tempered sampler runs under the same chain policy as the default sampler (see Chains and convergence policy below): two independently seeded chains by default, the drift check and the between-chain R-hat gate on the same monitored set, extensions of every chain and the same chain fields. A chain is extended, and lame_resume continues a fit, from its complete replica state (every replica, the step sizes and both random-number streams), so an extended chain is exactly the chain an uninterrupted run would have produced.

This route accepts only its documented factor and additive prior settings; Sab0 must be a positive multiple of the two by two identity and ab_var_cap must be infinite. Nodal covariates, changing actor sets, time-varying coefficients/factors, exposure, and chunked likelihood output are not supported. save_log_lik = TRUE stores one column per observed unordered dyad-period, also the unit counted by nobs(). Posterior storage uses the same posterior_opts interface, and compact joint terminal states are always retained for forecasts. LFO training windows need at least two periods. Tempered checkpoints restore every replica, the frozen model/prior and both random-number streams; only sampling length, output and time-limit settings can change on continuation. Built-in RNGs with serializable state are supported; Box-Muller and user-supplied RNGs are refused with an error.

Dynamic Effects Implementation:

The dynamic_uv and dynamic_ab parameters enable time-varying latent representations through autoregressive processes. These extensions are particularly useful for understanding how network structure evolves over time.

Dynamic Multiplicative Effects (dynamic_uv=TRUE):

The latent factors U and V evolve according to the transition selected by dynamic_uv_kind. The default "ar1" model uses Gaussian AR(1) drift: $$U_{i,k,t} = \rho_{uv} U_{i,k,t-1} + \epsilon_{i,k,t}$$ where \(\epsilon_{i,k,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{uv}^2)\), i indexes actors, k indexes latent dimensions, and t indexes time. The parameter \(\rho_{uv}\) controls temporal persistence (values near 1 indicate slow evolution). This captures time-varying homophily, latent community structure, and transitivity dynamics. The "snap" transition uses a mixture of AR(1) drift and discontinuous reset transitions, while "t" uses heavy-tailed Student-t innovations represented by local transition scales: given its scale \(\lambda_{i,t} \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\nu/2, \nu/2)\) (\(\nu\) = prior$t_nu), the innovation of actor i at period t is \(N(0, \sigma_{uv}^2 / \lambda_{i,t})\). In the MCMC sampler the first period is Student-t with the same \(\nu\) and the stationary scale \(\sigma_{uv} / \sqrt{1 - \rho_{uv}^2}\), drawn as \(N(0, \sigma_{uv}^2 / ((1 - \rho_{uv}^2) \lambda_{i,1}))\) with its own scale \(\lambda_{i,1}\), so that it has the tail of the transitions; the ALS estimator keeps a Gaussian first period. On the MCMC path, snap transitions are supported for directed, bipartite and symmetric models and t transitions for directed unipartite models, at any rank. With method = "als", Student-t dynamic UV is supported for directed and symmetric normal, binary, and Poisson panels, including named panels where actors enter or exit; the snap kind has no ALS route.

Key references:

  • Sewell & Chen (2015): Introduced dynamic latent space models with actor-specific evolution rates

  • Durante & Dunson (2014): Nonparametric Bayesian approach allowing flexible evolution of network structure

  • Hoff (2011): Hierarchical multilinear models providing theoretical foundation for temporal dependencies

Dynamic Additive Effects (dynamic_ab=TRUE): Each sender (a) and receiver (b) effect is a per-actor level plus a zero-mean AR(1) deviation: $$a_{i,t} = \mu^a_i + d_{i,t}, \quad d_{i,t} = \rho_{ab} d_{i,t-1} + \epsilon_{i,t}$$ $$b_{j,t} = \mu^b_j + e_{j,t}, \quad e_{j,t} = \rho_{ab} e_{j,t-1} + \eta_{j,t}$$ where \(\epsilon_{i,t}, \eta_{j,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{ab}^2)\). The variance of the levels across actors is the reported va / vb; \(\rho_{ab}\) and \(\sigma_{ab}\) describe the deviations. This models time-varying individual activity levels (outdegree) and popularity (indegree).

Identified reporting: Stored static factor draws are centered only when both resolved actor margins are enabled. The removed row, column and grand-mean components of \(U G V'\) are transferred to the actor effects and intercept; for a symmetric shared actor without an intercept, the grand constant is divided equally between its two contributions. Otherwise, the saved draws retain their sampled coordinates because disabled effects cannot absorb the offsets. The reported map preserves the linear predictor and leaves the sampler state unchanged. Dynamic-coordinate reporting follows the supported fitted route; inspect fitted products and predictions when comparing latent geometries.

Dynamic additive effects are useful when sender activity and receiver popularity change over time rather than staying fixed across the whole panel. A dynamic_ab fit returns the posterior-mean paths on fit$a_dynamic / fit$b_dynamic (actor x period) and their per-period posterior standard deviations on fit$a_dynamic_sd / fit$b_dynamic_sd; ab_plot(fit, plot_type = "ribbon") uses the latter to draw a credible band around each actor's path.

Prior Specification for Dynamic Parameters:

  • \(\rho_{uv}, \rho_{ab} \sim TruncNormal(mean, sd, -0.99, 0.99)\): Ensures stationarity of AR(1) process

  • \(\sigma_{uv}^2 / (1 - \rho_{uv}^2) \sim InverseGamma(shape, scale)\) independently of \(\rho_{uv}\): the stationary variance of a coordinate path (prior$uv_var_shape, prior$uv_var_scale)

  • \(\sigma_{ab}^2 \sim InverseGamma(shape, scale)\): Controls innovation variance

  • Default priors (\(\rho_{uv}\) mean=0.7, sd=0.3; \(\rho_{ab}\) mean=0.8) favor persistent evolution

  • Adjust rho_*_mean closer to 1 for slower evolution, closer to 0 for more rapid changes

Computational Considerations:

  • Dynamic effects add path updates; runtime depends on actor count, rank and number of periods

  • Memory usage scales as O(nRT) for dynamic_uv, O(n*T) for dynamic_ab

  • C++ implementation is substantially faster than a pure R loop

  • Convergence diagnostics: Monitor rho and sigma parameters carefully

  • Effective sample sizes typically lower due to temporal correlation

  • A chain that is still moving when the run ends is continued, and refused if it keeps moving (see the convergence policy below)

Chains and convergence policy: lame() runs chains chains (default 2; options(lame.chains = k) sets another default). Chain \(k\) is seeded with seed + 1000 * (k - 1), so chains = 1 is the first chain of a two-chain fit. On Unix the chains run forked, on at most cores workers (all cores but one by default); on Windows they run one after the other. The draws do not depend on the number of workers. The result is the pooled fit of combine_ame_chains, with fit$chains, fit$chain_seeds, fit$rhat (the R-hat of each monitored series with its effective draws per split chain, pooled ess and of the least-mixing chain ess_chain, its threshold, whether the chains hold enough effective draws to be compared on it, informative, and how many that takes, ess_needed), the state each chain stopped in, and the chain_indicator that as_draws() and trace_plot use. Two chains cost twice the CPU time and about the same wall time on a multicore machine.

At the end of the post-burn run every chain is checked, and the chains are compared with each other. Within a chain, the first and last thirds of the stored draws of the intercept (or first coefficient), va, vb, ve, rho, rho_ab, sigma_ab, rho_uv, sigma_uv and pi_snap are compared with batch-means standard errors (ten batches per third); a quantity is flagged when the two means differ by more than half a posterior standard deviation of the whole series and by more standard errors than the drift threshold. Between chains, the split rank-normalised R-hat (Vehtari et al., 2021) of each series of the monitored set is compared with its threshold. Both thresholds are set so that chance alone flags settled chains anywhere in the fit with probability about 1 percent per check, however many quantities are checked. The chains are compared on a series only when they hold enough effective draws for its threshold to catch chains one posterior standard deviation apart at least 95 percent of the time; a series with fewer is flagged as having too few effective draws to compare (see Gate thresholds below). The monitored set is every regression coefficient (each period's under dynamic_beta), va, vb, cab, ve, rho, the dynamic hyperparameters, and summaries of the additive and latent structure recorded at every stored draw (the rms of a and b, the largest actor effect, the rms of the latent product \(UGV'\), the norm of G of a bipartite fit and the split of scale between U and V of a directed fit, per period for dynamic fits). The dyadic products are not monitored. Quantities a fit reports as not estimated are left out, and a run with fewer than 60 stored draws per chain is not checked (print() says so). The gate is computed on the draws the returned fit holds (the last block of every chain). fit$diagnostics$rhat, from compute_mcmc_diagnostics, is the same statistic of the same draws and equals fit$rhat for every monitored coefficient and variance component.

When a chain drifts, an R-hat exceeds its threshold or a series has too few effective draws to compare, every chain is extended by a block of sweeps from its own final state, as lame_resume does (the seeds advance by the sweeps already run); the flagged block counts as extra burn-in, its draws are discarded, and both checks run again. The block is nscan sweeps or, when series are short of effective draws, long enough for each to hold a quarter more than it needs at its autocorrelation (at most four times nscan; the stored draws grow with the block). Up to prior$chain_extensions extensions are made (default 3). The returned fit holds the draws of the last block, and fit$auto_extend records the extensions, the sweeps discarded, the length of the last block (block_nscan) and the quantities that triggered each. If a chain of the last block still drifts or an R-hat is still above its threshold, lame() stops with an error of class lame_chain_unsettled: its fits field holds the chains, fit the pooled fit of the last block, rhat the monitored table (R-hat, effective draws, threshold and verdict of every series) and moving the offending quantities with the reason, and lame_resume(e$fit, nscan = nscan) continues every chain (lame_resume(e$fits[[k]], nscan = nscan) one). If the chains of the last block only hold too few effective draws on some series, the fit is returned with a warning of class lame_chain_not_compared that names them and the nscan that would be enough, and fit$rhat marks them informative = FALSE. prior = list(chain_extensions = 0) decides on the first block; chains = 1 runs one chain with the drift check only. No fit is returned with a drifting chain or an R-hat above its threshold.

Gate thresholds. Each quantity is tested on its own, so a fixed threshold flags settled chains more often the more quantities are monitored and the fewer effective draws they hold. Both checks therefore use thresholds for the whole fit at the family-wise level \(\alpha = 0.01\). With \(m\) tests, each is made at the Sidak level \(a = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^{1/m}\). The drift threshold is the two-sided \(a\) quantile of Student's t on the Welch degrees of freedom of the two batch-means errors, \(m\) counting every quantity of every chain, and never below 3. For R-hat, \(m\) is twice the number of compared series (bulk and tail R-hat). For \(K\) split chains of \(n\) draws holding \(e\) effective draws each (pooled over the chains, from the autocorrelation within each chain of the rank-normalised draws by Geyer's initial monotone sequence), settled chains have a squared split R-hat of about \((n - 1)/n \, (1 + F/(e - 1))\), with \(F\) distributed as \(F(K - 1, K(e - 1))\); the threshold of a series is the larger of 1.05 and this value at the \(1 - a\) quantile of \(F\). Two chains \(d\) posterior standard deviations apart make \(F\) noncentral, with noncentrality \(e d^2\). The chains are compared on a series when its threshold flags \(d = 1\) with probability at least 0.95, which takes about 35 effective draws per split chain with 12 compared series, 38 with 30 and 41 with 100, almost whatever the run length; the threshold of a compared series is then between 1.05 and about 1.09. A series with fewer effective draws is flagged as too few to compare, and one whose R-hat exceeds even the wider threshold of its effective draws as disagreeing. The pooled effective draws are those of the comparison (the difference of two chain means varies as for chains holding the harmonic mean of their effective draws), so one sticky chain beside a mixing one leaves too few. Chains constant on a series at different values have an infinite R-hat and are flagged; chains constant at one value pass. The threshold falls and the power rises with the effective draws, and at a fixed autocorrelation time with the run length, so settled chains are extended less often, and chains one standard deviation apart flagged at least 95 percent of the time, the more or the better mixing their draws.

A split chain of \(n\) stored draws holds at most \(n\) effective draws, so in a first block of 100 stored draws per chain (nscan = 2000, odens = 20) the chains can be compared only on series whose draws are nearly independent (an autocorrelation time up to about 1.3 stored draws, a lag-one autocorrelation of about 0.14 for an autoregressive series), and at the defaults (400 stored draws per chain) on series with an autocorrelation time up to about 5 (lag-one about 0.68); the longer extension blocks (up to four times as long) take these to about 4 and 17 stored draws (lag-one about 0.6 and 0.89). No comparison of two chains does much better: the z test of the difference of the chain means with the variance known needs 27 effective draws per split chain to find a one standard deviation separation 95 percent of the time at the family-wise level 1 percent over 30 series.

Measured on two-chain blocks cut from long stationary runs of six simulated configurations (static and dynamic, normal, binary "t" kind, Poisson, bipartite Poisson and frn; 12 to 48 monitored series), no block of 400 stored draws per chain had an R-hat above its threshold, and 4 of the 48 bipartite Poisson blocks (none of the other 163) had too few effective draws on rho_uv; at 100 stored draws per chain 79 percent of the static normal blocks and every block of the other five had too few on some series. On 30 settled autoregressive series per fit, chance put an R-hat above its threshold on at most 0.5 percent of series at every lag-one autocorrelation from 0 to 0.95 and both lengths; a fit of 400 stored draws per chain was extended for too few effective draws in 0 percent of fits up to 0.3, 2 percent at 0.5, 77 percent at 0.6 and every fit from 0.7, and one of 100 stored draws in every fit. A one standard deviation separation on one series was flagged in at least 98 percent of fits at every autocorrelation and length, and in at least 96 percent of those in which the chains could be compared.

Rerun with the seeds and settings of the release sweep (burn = 500, nscan = 2000, odens = 20, two chains) on 63 fits that the fixed thresholds had refused or extended, the gate refused none. 48 passed, every one after one or two longer blocks (100 stored draws per chain leave most series too few effective draws), with a largest R-hat of 1.056 and at least 39 effective draws per split chain. 15 were returned with too few effective draws on some series: all 8 fits whose directed scale split was left to the conditional updates (uv_split_move = FALSE; uv_split held 6 to 13 effective draws per split chain after four blocks) and 7 of the 11 snap fits (uv_rms and uv_split, 4 to 36). With the earlier thresholds the same draws gave 11 refusals, all among those 15 fits and one snap fit that passes once its chains run longer.

The dyadic products are left out because their largest R-hat crosses 1.05 on settled chains. A fit has about \(10^4\) of them, and on stationary chains of 17 simulated configurations with a latent product (68 two-chain blocks) the largest product R-hat of a block reached 1.055; settled ordinal directed fits with dynamic_uv crossed 1.05 in 2 of their 4 blocks, so a product gate at 1.05 would extend and refuse settled fits. In the three acceptance configurations whose products failed the book's gate at the defaults (a Poisson undirected static rank-2 fit, and frn and ordinal directed fits with dynamic_uv), the smallest product effective sample size of a failing run was 19 to 87 of 800 draws. Run at four times the default nscan, all three passed, and the posterior-mean product fit$UVPM moved by at most 0.27 posterior standard deviations on any dyad. A study that reports individual dyadic products, rather than fit$UVPM or the monitored summaries, keeps the position draws (posterior_opts = list(save_UV = TRUE)) and continues the chains with lame_resume() until the R-hat of every reported product is below 1.05.

Model Selection Guidelines: Use both dynamic_uv and dynamic_ab when:

  • Networks show clear temporal trends in density or clustering

  • Individual node behavior changes systematically over time

  • Community structure evolves (merging, splitting, drift)

Use only dynamic_uv when:

  • Latent structure/communities change but individual effects are stable

  • Focus is on evolving homophily or clustering patterns

  • Network shows structural reconfiguration over time

Use only dynamic_ab when:

  • Individual heterogeneity varies but overall structure is stable

  • Actors' activity/popularity changes over observation period

  • Focus is on individual-level temporal dynamics

Bipartite Network Models:

When mode="bipartite", the model handles rectangular adjacency matrices Y with dimensions n_A x n_B, where n_A and n_B represent the number of row and column nodes respectively.

Static Bipartite Case: The model uses separate latent factor matrices:

  • U: n_A x R_row matrix of row node latent positions

  • V: n_B x R_col matrix of column node latent positions

  • G: R_row x R_col interaction matrix mapping between latent spaces

  • Multiplicative term: U G V' captures bipartite community structure

Dynamic Bipartite Case: When dynamic_uv=TRUE for bipartite networks: $$U_{i,k,t} = \rho_{uv} U_{i,k,t-1} + \epsilon_{i,k,t}$$ $$V_{j,k,t} = \rho_{uv} V_{j,k,t-1} + \eta_{j,k,t}$$ where i indexes row nodes, j indexes column nodes, k indexes latent dimensions.

Every bipartite fit estimates a single interaction matrix and returns it as fit$G: with moving positions a per-period interaction matrix is not identified apart from them (\(U_t G_t V_t'\) and \((U_t G_t) V_t'\) describe the same products). Use dynamic_uv = TRUE for a time-varying multiplicative term and read the per-period product fit$UVPM, which is the identified quantity.

Key Differences from Unipartite Models:

  • No dyadic correlation (rho): Bipartite edges are inherently directed

  • Separate dimensions: R_row and R_col can differ for row/column spaces

  • Rectangular structure: Network density patterns differ from square matrices

  • Community interpretation: Captures affiliation patterns between node types

Missing covariates:

A cell whose dyadic covariate, sender (row) covariate or receiver (column) covariate is missing in its period is an unobserved tie, for unipartite and bipartite panels alike: it is set to NA in Y before the design is built, and the covariate coefficients are estimated from the complete cells. A message gives the number of such cells. A missing value is never modelled as 0, which would bias the coefficient of a covariate that is not centred. In a symmetric panel a dyad has one covariate value: a hole in one triangle of a dyadic covariate is filled from the other triangle (a message gives the number of values), so the slice stays symmetric and the dyad stays observed, and a dyad missing in both triangles is unobserved. A missing node covariate removes the actor's row and column in that period. A covariate that is missing in every period stops the fit. ame and the ALS routes apply the same rule and give the same messages.

Collinear covariates:

A regression design whose columns are aliased over the observed cells of the whole panel (a covariate that duplicates another, or one that is a linear combination of others, counting the intercept and the sender and receiver covariates), static or with dynamic_beta, is an error of class lame_design_rank. It names the aliased columns and the combination each equals: the data cannot separate their coefficients, so the posterior along that direction would be the prior's alone. The periods are pooled, so a covariate that duplicates another in some periods only is fitted, and period indicators that span the intercept still drop it, with the warning. A column is aliased when it is a combination of the columns before it to a relative 1.5e-7, the collinearity below which the cross products the coefficient updates work with keep fewer than two digits; a design that is only nearly collinear is fitted. method = "als" refuses the same designs with the same condition (fields aliased, rank and n_col) for every estimator and family.

Standard AME Model Types:

The following describes the six standard data types/models available:

"normal": A normal AME model.

"binary": A binary probit AME model.

"ordinal": An ordinal probit AME model. An intercept is not identifiable with data-induced cutpoints. Explicit cutpoints anchored at zero support an intercept.

"cbin": An AME model for censored binary data. The value of 'odmax' specifies the maximum number of links each row may have.

"frn": An AME model for fixed rank nomination networks. A higher value of the rank indicates a stronger relationship. The value of 'odmax' specifies the maximum number of links each row may have.

For both families a missing cell (NA) of an actor present in the period is an unobserved nomination or non-nomination: it counts against its row's cap while it holds a nomination, and the sampler draws it from its conditional given the row's observed cells. A row at its cap is bounded below only, so the sweep moves its level slowly; each sender's level is therefore also moved together with its latent row once per sweep, drawn from its conditional. On simulated designs (30 actors and one period, 24 actors and two to six, cap 10, more than 3,000 fits) the 95 percent intervals of vb and cab covered 0.97 to 1.00 of the panels at every share of rows at the cap, with and without a fifth of the cells hidden, and those of va 0.90 to 1.00 outside the region odmax describes and 0.91 inside it. Two designs withhold the level of the rows (see odmax): one period, where a row at its cap shows only that its level fills the cap, with every row at the cap, or with cells hidden and a share at the cap from 0.5 (the intercept interval covered 0.64 and 0.84 of the panels; ame() and one-period lame() report the intercept and any row-covariate coefficient as not estimated then); and two periods or more with a share from 0.5 and a posterior-mean va from 0.5 to 1.5. At a generating sender sd of 0.25 the posterior mean of va runs up to 2.3 times the generating variance while the interval still covers. fit$hidden_cell_ess records the effective sample size of the intercept and va of a fit with hidden cells. The posterior predictive (YPM, fitted(), the goodness-of-fit replicates and simulate()) lets a missing cell hold a nomination, as the sampler does, so YPM also predicts those cells; the diagonal and the cells of an actor absent from the period are left out.

"poisson": An overdispersed Poisson-lognormal model for counts (negative or non-integer observed values are an error): \(Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(e \exp(z))\) with \(z \sim N(\eta, \sigma^2)\). Given \(\eta\) and \(\sigma^2\), a cell's mean count is \(e \exp(\eta + \sigma^2/2)\). YPM, fitted() and predict(type = "response") report it, for the exposure \(e_t\) of the period (period_exposure; one without), at the posterior mean \(\eta\) of the linear predictor (EZ) and the posterior mean \(\sigma^2\) of the residual variance, the form the fast estimators report. Predictive quantiles and event probabilities come from posterior predictive draws (simulate(), predict(fit, h = 1, interval = "prediction")). Zero exposure gives a structural zero count.

Joint scale move (binary, unipartite and bipartite):

A probit panel identifies the scale of the linear predictor only weakly: a higher intercept with less spread in the additive effects and smaller latent positions fits a sparse panel nearly as well, so the level of the predictor and the spread of the effects trade off along a ridge. The conditional sweep cannot step along it, because conditioning on the latent \(Z\) pins the scale of every block, and a cold start can take many thousands of sweeps to arrive. Binary unipartite fits therefore carry a Metropolis step that multiplies the coefficients and additive effects by a factor \(c\) and the latent positions by \(\sqrt{c}\), with the variance parameters held fixed over the step and following it through their own draws. Under dynamic_ab the same visit walks a second direction: the per-period deviations of the additive effects together with \(\sigma_{ab}\), whose amplitude relative to that innovation scale is a ridge of its own (the deviation draw pins the deviations given \(\sigma_{ab}\) and its draw pins \(\sigma_{ab}\) given them). Moving the two together leaves their AR(1) prior invariant, so only the likelihood and the inverse-gamma prior on \(\sigma_{ab}^2\) resist; set prior$dev_move = FALSE to leave that direction out. The step integrates \(Z\) out (the dyad errors are split into a shared factor and an independent part; the factor is drawn from its conditional and the independent part integrated out), so it is accepted against the exact conditional posterior and leaves it unchanged; \(Z\) is redrawn from its conditional when the step is accepted. It is visited every prior$level_move_every sweeps (default 30) with prior$level_move_tries proposals per visit (default 8), adapts its step size during burn-in only, and reports its acceptance rate in fit$level_move. It is off for other families, symmetric fits and dynamic_rho. Changing coefficients with static factors are supported for ranks 1 and 2 when both actor margins and dynamic_ab are enabled, dcor = FALSE, and the coefficient law is AR(1) or RW1 on the regular grid, with zero initial means and diagonal innovation scaling. The static factor covariance is integrated in the acceptance density.

That configuration also receives a joint Hamiltonian update of coefficients, actor effects and factors with the binary latent responses integrated out. It requires at least three actors and one static coefficient. The update uses exact actor contrasts, keeps hyperparameters fixed, and adapts its step size during burn-in only. Bounded momentum kicks preserve reversal and phase-space volume; the Metropolis correction retains the original target. It runs every 20 sweeps; acceptance and numerical rejections are recorded in fit$marginal_move. Set prior$marginal_move = FALSE to omit this update. With static additive effects, an intercept, both actor margins and the same rank-one or rank-two changing-coefficient configuration, a joint observed-data update moves static actor contrasts, coefficients and factors. It integrates out the static factor covariance under its original prior. Bounded momentum updates and a Metropolis correction preserve the original target. The move begins after half of burn-in and runs every 20 sweeps; its step size adapts only during burn-in. Acceptance and numerical rejections are recorded in fit$marginal_move. Set prior$marginal_move = FALSE to omit this static-actor update.

Other changing-coefficient and static-factor configurations retain their existing updates.

Binary bipartite fits with an intercept, both margins, static coefficients and, when they have a multiplicative term, a static interaction matrix carry the same step on the whole predictor: the coefficients, the additive effects (and their deviations under dynamic_ab) and the interaction matrix \(G\) are multiplied by \(c\) with the latent positions held. The cells of a bipartite panel have no dyadic correlation, so no shared factor is drawn, and the prior terms of every block the factor touches (the coefficient prior, the effects, their AR(1) deviations, the \(N(0, 1)\) prior of the entries of \(G\) cut at prior$G_max) are included in the acceptance ratio.

Binary unipartite fits (directed or symmetric, with any additive margin in the model, and with static coefficients or dynamic_beta of kind "ar1" or "rw1") also receive a collapsed per-actor update. The data-augmentation sweep draws an actor's parameters from a normal whose precision is the number of cells the actor appears in, so an actor whose cells hold no events (a flat likelihood on a half line) moves by about \(1/\sqrt{m}\) per sweep however wide its posterior is, and relaxes in about \(v m\) sweeps: thousands of sweeps for the additive level of an inactive actor, and \(10^5\) for static positions that have spread out, because the positions also feed the factor covariance they are drawn under. The update integrates the latent array out (as the scale move does) and draws, one actor at a time, an exact elliptical slice step of the actor's sender and receiver level translations and, for static positions, of its sender and receiver positions. The level translation adds a constant to one actor's predictor while the other levels and the intercept absorb the re-centring, so it keeps the sum-to-zero constraint and touches one row (or column) of the likelihood. The latent array is redrawn afterwards, so the posterior is unchanged; there is nothing to tune. It is available for dynamic_ab and static effects, ranks 0 to any with static positions (positions that move over time keep their own updates; only the levels are moved), and is visited every prior$actor_move_every sweeps (default 10). The positions are left to the sampler during the first half of burn-in, when it runs under a fixed diffuse prior that lets the positions of actors without information take any scale. In a symmetric fit an actor has one level, which enters both its row and its column, and the positions are those of the eigenmodel (\(u_i\) with the diagonal weights held fixed during the visit, drawn under the sampler's own precision prior); there is no dyadic correlation. Panels with absent actors (changing composition) are covered: only observed cells enter a likelihood, an actor with no observed cell in a block has the prior as its conditional there and the slice step moves it across that prior, the translation moves the level of absent periods with the rest, and the missing cells are redrawn from the model afterwards, as the sampler does. Set prior$actor_move = FALSE to omit it; its work is recorded in fit$actor_move. For directed fits with dcor = TRUE the same visit also updates the dyadic correlation with both latent responses of each dyad integrated out (an independent proposal from its \(1 - \rho^2\) prior, accepted on the exact pair likelihood, followed by an exact redraw of the latent array), because given the augmented array the correlation moves by about \(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{dyads}}\) and mixes slowly when few dyads are mutual; prior$actor_move_rho = FALSE omits that part.

The Poisson and ordinal families have the same slow direction, and the latent array cannot be integrated out, so their update carries it along: an actor's level is translated together with the latent values of its row (its column, or the pairs of a symmetric network), which leaves every residual, hence the Gaussian density of the latent array, unchanged. The shift is then an exact draw from the level prior (with the intercept that absorbs the re-centring) times the data factor of the row: the log-concave Poisson factor of the observed cells (an elliptical slice step) or, for the ordinal family, the indicator that the shifted values keep their ranks (or stay inside their cutpoint intervals), which cuts the prior at both ends and is drawn as a truncated normal. The intercept, the spread of the levels and the levels of the inactive actors, which the sweep alone crosses over thousands of sweeps on a sparse panel, then mix within a few visits. With static coefficients the Poisson family also translates each coefficient with the latent array, and moves the dyadic variance and the dyadic correlation together with the latent residuals (a Metropolis step whose ratio is the change of the Poisson factor and the priors), because given the array the residuals are prior draws wherever the counts say little, and, with static positions, redraws each actor's position with the latent values of its row or column carried along (an elliptical slice step under the factor prior the sampler draws under; the positions are left to the sampler during the first half of burn-in, when it runs under a fixed diffuse prior); the ordinal family draws the location of the latent array (the means of the levels, or the intercept), which the rank likelihood leaves free and explicit cutpoints confine to a strip. Visits are every prior$actor_move_every sweeps (default 10).

With moving positions (dynamic_uv = TRUE with a positive rank, of the "ar1" and "snap" kinds, or the "t" kind of a directed network) the sweep moves the position path of an actor whose cells say little (no events, or absent from most periods) by a step of about \(\sqrt{s_2 / m}\) per sweep, \(m\) the number of its cells, however wide the posterior of the path is (\(s_2\) is the dyadic variance, near 0.05 for a sparse Poisson panel and 1 for the probit families). The paths of such actors then wander at no likelihood cost, and the squared product of the positions, the persistence and innovation scale of the paths and the intercept follow them with autocorrelation times of hundreds to thousands of sweeps. Every prior$actor_move_every sweeps the update therefore redraws each actor's whole path, the senders' and then the receivers' (a symmetric network's once), with one elliptical slice step under the AR(1) prior of the path (stationary start; the local innovation scales of the "t" kind), the persistence and the innovation scale being held. For the Poisson family the latent values of the actor's row or column are moved with the predictor, which changes no residual, so the conditional of the path is its prior times the Poisson factor of the cells. For the binary family the latent array is integrated out as in the collapsed update above (the shared dyad factor of a directed network is drawn once per visit, each observed cell contributes a probit factor, and the latent array is redrawn at the end). Bipartite fits use their interaction matrix and symmetric fits the signed weights of their unit-variance coordinate paths. A directed binary fit with dynamic_ab at rank two already has the paired-actor slice step described below and is left to it; ordinal fits keep the sampler's own updates. Under the "snap" kind every family takes a compiled visit of the paths (every sweep; Poisson fits with their translations): binary and Poisson fits with the factors above, the normal, ordinal, "cbin" and "frn" families with the latent array held and the Gaussian density of each latent cell given its reciprocal partner (bipartite and symmetric cells have none; a symmetric actor's line holds each of its pairs once, and the visit moves both triangles and the diagonal). A bipartite fit visits its row and then its column paths, each with its own resets, through \(G\); a symmetric fit visits its one set of unit-variance paths through their weights. Each path takes five exact steps given the rest of the state. Its prior with the resets summed out is \(N(x_1; 0, \sigma^2 / (1 - \rho^2) I) \prod_t m(x_t \mid x_{t-1})\), \(m(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = (1 - \pi) N(\rho x_{t-1}, \sigma^2 I) + \pi N(0, \kappa^2 I)\): (1) a slice step under a Gaussian reference prior, the AR(1) path or with equal chance the path that resets at one later period, whose likelihood is the factor of the cells times the ratio of the two priors, so the step can open or close a reset; (2) Metropolis steps on \(\log c\) for \(x_s \to c x_s\), \(s \ge t_0\) with \(t_0\) drawn at random, with the Jacobian \(c^{R (N - t_0 + 1)}\), which crosses the width of a reset position; (3) the resets given the path; (4) a slice step given the resets; (5) the resets again. The sampler's own update draws an actor's reset and position for one period at a time given the latent array and the neighbouring periods, so on its own it rarely passes between a reset and a drift explanation of a period change. Given the resets the prior of the paths is Gaussian, with each reset position entering the moments of the paths at weight \(\sigma^2 / \kappa^2\) and no transition from the period before, so the exact gauge moves of bipartite and symmetric paths (the scale split, the common gauge against \(G\), the split of a symmetric column against its weight, the period signs and the signs along the singular directions of \(G\)) read those moments, and the persistence of symmetric paths is drawn from their drifting transitions alone (the first period and, under the linked scale of 1, a reset position do not depend on it). A symmetric "ar1" Poisson or binary fit also draws, every sweep, the scale ridge between its coordinate paths and their weights (scaling a coordinate of every path by \(c\) and its weight by \(1/c^2\) changes no cell of the predictor, so the draw is a Metropolis step on \(\log c\) with the ratio of the priors; it is recorded as dpm_scale_attempts and dpm_scale_accepts) and draws the persistence rho_uv with a proposal scale taken from the transitions of the paths, where the fixed scale of the sampler's own draw is 10 to 90 times the width of the conditional at persistences from 0.9 to 0.985 and moves rho_uv in one call of every ten to ninety. prior$actor_move_paths = FALSE omits this part only.

With dynamic_beta the prior of the intercept enters the density of a level translation through its path: the translation moves the whole path by the same constant, which changes the prior of the first state and, unless the path is a random walk, of the transitions. A static intercept next to moving coefficients enters through its own prior, and moving coefficients other than the intercept are not touched. A fit with no additive margin (rvar = cvar = FALSE, or a symmetric fit with nvar = FALSE) and static positions runs the position steps alone, and a fit with one margin translates the levels of that margin. Coefficient paths of the other kinds ("rw2", "matern32") or on a non-unit period grid keep their own updates.

The same update runs for bipartite binary fits (and in ame for a bipartite cross-section): each row and column actor's level translation, which moves the intercept with it and touches one row or column of the likelihood, and, for static positions, its position, as exact elliptical slice draws with the latent array integrated out; under dynamic_ab it also draws the deviation paths of random pairs of actors of a margin with their sum held. A bipartite cell has no partner cell, so there is no reciprocity update, and the positions have a fixed unit-variance prior, so there is no factor covariance to draw. Missing cells and the cells of an actor absent from a period carry no likelihood, and the update is never switched off by missingness. With dynamic_beta of kind "ar1" or "rw1" on the unit period grid the translation moves the whole intercept path by the same constant (a static intercept next to moving coefficients by the same amount), and the prior of the intercept enters the density of the translation through its path, as for unipartite fits.

A "poisson" fit translates the coefficients that move as well. The counts of a period fix the log of its mean to about \(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{events}}\), while given the latent array the intercept of the period is known to \(\sqrt{s^2/\mathrm{cells}}\), 10 to 20 times less on a sparse panel (0.015 to 0.022 against 0.0012 at 170 actors); the sweep moved the intercepts of the periods, and with them the coefficient of a dyadic covariate and the dyadic variance and correlation, by random walk. The gate panel of 170 actors and four periods had 3 to 14 effective draws of the period intercepts in 1,600 (split R-hat 1.5), 6 of the covariate coefficient, 6 of the correlation and 16 of the variance. Raising coefficient \(k\) of one period by \(\delta\) and the latent values of the period by \(\delta x_{kt}\) leaves every residual unchanged, so the shift is an exact draw (an elliptical slice step) from the prior of the shifted path times the log-concave Poisson factor of the period's cells. The prior is the one of the path's kind ("ar1", "rw1", "rw2", "matern32", on any time grid), read from the precision the path sampler uses. The whole path of a coefficient is translated the same way, and so are the static coefficients next to moving ones, with the latent array of every period, at the visits of the translations of the actor levels (prior$poisson_period_move = FALSE and prior$poisson_static_move = FALSE omit them). Those fits, and every other "poisson" fit without dynamic_rho, then move the dyadic variance and correlation at every sweep with the latent residuals carried along their conditional law: given the counts the residuals of a dyad are close to a Gaussian with mean \(m\) and covariance \(V\) (the Gaussian prior times the first-order terms of the Poisson factors), the move maps \(e' = m' + L'L^{-1}(e - m)\) for a proposed variance and correlation, and accepts with the Metropolis ratio of the joint density (the change of the Poisson factors, of the Gaussian density and the Jacobian of the map). The residuals of the cells with a count are tilted by about \(s^2 (y - \lambda)\), which follows the variance and not its square root, so scaling them as the translations of the actor levels do accepts steps of a few hundredths in the log variance, and this map accepts steps of 0.1 to 0.8. The visits of the translations of the actor levels are every second sweep for the Poisson family (every tenth left the least active actors with 30 to 80 effective draws of 2,000); fit$poisson_period_move records the moves. On the gate panel the period intercepts then have 1,370 to 1,450 effective draws of 1,600, the covariate coefficient 1,320, the correlation 650, the variance 850 and the slowest actor effect 400, and the split R-hat is 1.006; a sweep takes about a third longer.

An "ordinal" fit draws the scale of its latent array along the transformations that keep every rank. With the default data-induced cutpoints a cell of the latent array is drawn between the extreme values of the neighbouring categories, and those extremes are order statistics of thousands of cells: they move by steps of \(1/\mathrm{cells}\) per sweep, while the scale of the whole configuration (the spread of the implied cutpoints against the unit residual variance) has a posterior of width \(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{cells}}\), and given the latent array the coefficients, the additive effects and the dyadic correlation are tied to it. On 150 actors the coefficient of a dyadic covariate had 8 effective draws of 600 and the correlation 95; on 100 actors in four periods, whose rank windows are separate, 3 of 400 and 3. Multiplying the latent array, the coefficients and the static additive effects by a factor \(c\) keeps every rank, and \(c\) has an exact conditional (a group move whose invariant measure is \(dc/c\): a gamma draw when the priors have mean zero and the predictor is fully scaled, an independence Metropolis step from its Laplace approximation otherwise). The shift and the scale of the latent array of each period alone keep that period's ranks and have exact conditionals too. Both are drawn at every sweep, and the same panels then have 600 and 400 effective draws of the coefficient and 400 and 270 of the correlation. The multiplicative effects, the dynamic additive effects and the dynamic positions stay unscaled parts of the predictor: the moves stay exact, and their efficiency is the share of the signal they scale. With explicit cutpoints the scale of the whole state carries the free cutpoints with it; the cutpoints of a directed fit with dcor = TRUE are drawn given the latent array, and on 50 actors the coefficient had 56 effective draws of 500 and the correlation 47, now 440 and 290 (prior$ordinal_scale_move = FALSE omits the moves; fit$ordinal_scale_move records them).

A "binary" fit draws the scale of its linear predictor with the latent array integrated out. When a covariate separates the ties (every tie lies above every non-tie on it) the likelihood increases without a bound along the ray that multiplies the coefficients and the additive effects by a factor \(c > 1\), and the posterior of the coefficient is its prior times a likelihood that saturates only where the dyads nearest the boundary are classified. The data-augmentation sweep draws every block given the latent array and crosses that direction by steps of \(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{cells}}\): on a 30-actor directed panel the separating coefficient had 12 effective draws of 2,000 (steps of 0.03 against a posterior sd of 0.6), and on a bipartite panel, whose coefficients have the independent prior \(N(0, g)\) with \(g\) the number of cells, it was still climbing after 8,000 sweeps (14.0 and 15.6 for two seeds, against a posterior mean of 59). Every prior$binary_scale_every-th sweep (default 5) the coefficients and the static additive effects are therefore multiplied by a factor drawn exactly from its conditional density, a group move whose invariant measure is \(dc/c\): the dyad errors of a directed network are split into a shared factor, drawn from its conditional given the latent array, and independent parts that are integrated out, so that each cell contributes one probit factor, and the latent array is redrawn from its conditional afterwards (the device of the collapsed actor updates). The multiplicative effects, the dynamic additive effects and the actor-specific slopes stay where they are and the draw stays exact; its efficiency is the share of the signal it scales. The same panels then have 460 and 140 effective draws of 2,000 after 8,000 sweeps, two seeds agree, and the posterior mean is the same at 2,000, 8,000 and 32,000 sweeps.
