The draw runs in every binary configuration of ame() and lame() except dynamic_rho, next to the joint scale move and the Hamiltonian updates described above where those run: in the Hamiltonian configuration (changing coefficients and effects, rank one) the separating coefficient had 16 to 20 effective draws of 2,000 after 8,000 sweeps (the two seeds agreed on its mean to within the Monte Carlo error) and now has 1,000 to 1,200, and in the static directed configuration 140 to 200 and now 630 to 910. prior$binary_scale_move = FALSE omits it; fit$binary_scale_move records it.

The actor-period effects of a "poisson" fit with dynamic_ab are moved together with the latent values of their rows and columns. Given the latent array an effect has the precision of the cells it touches over the residual variance, so a Poisson panel of sparse counts moved the effects, and with them the innovation scale sigma_ab, the persistence and the levels, by small steps (on 50 actors in five periods sigma_ab had 6 to 34 effective draws of 800 and the effects of the first and last period, whose paths have one neighbour, R-hat up to 1.34). Each sweep moves an effect and the latent values of its row by one amount, the cell residuals staying where they are, so that the conditional is the prior of the effect given its neighbours and level times a Poisson factor that is two sums per row; the draw is an elliptical slice step, and with an intercept the effects of a period are moved in pairs, which keeps their sum. sigma_ab then has 216 to 311 effective draws (prior$ab_period_move = FALSE omits the move; fit$ab_period_move records it).

Under dynamic_ab (every family; bipartite, directed and symmetric unipartite networks) the effect of an actor in a period is a level plus a stationary AR(1) deviation, and the likelihood sees only their sum, so a short or sparse panel splits the common variance of the effects between the level variance and a persistent deviation almost freely, and the sweep, which draws the levels given the hyperparameters and the hyperparameters given the levels, crosses that ridge only over thousands of sweeps. Each sweep therefore draws the level variances (for a directed network their covariance, the pair of an actor's levels being correlated), the innovation scale and the persistence from their density given the totals, with the levels integrated out, before the levels are redrawn from their conditional. The update uses only the totals, so it needs no latent array and does not depend on the family, leaves the posterior unchanged and is recorded in fit$ab_hyper_move; prior$ab_hyper_move = FALSE omits it and prior$ab_hyper_move_tries sets the proposals per sweep (default 8). For bipartite fits with static positions the scale of the positions trades against the scale of the interaction matrix, which the unit priors anchor weakly. Each sweep also draws, exactly from its conditional, the factors by which the columns of the positions and the rows and columns of the interaction matrix are rescaled, and the shears between columns of a side (each a Gaussian draw), without changing their product (recorded in fit$uv_g_scale_move; prior$uv_g_scale_move = FALSE omits it).

Directed "cbin" and "frn" fits receive a receiver-level counterpart of the update their sender levels already have, which translates a sender's level together with its whole latent row. The data-augmentation sweep alone moves a receiver's level and its latent column by about \(1/\sqrt{m}\) per sweep, \(m\) the number of cells in the column, however wide the posterior is, and for a receiver nobody nominates (a column bounded above only) the effective sample size of the level falls roughly as \(1/n\). One sweep of the update visits each receiver once and translates its level and its latent column by the same amount. Every residual is unchanged, so the amount enters the density only through the prior of the shifted level and the order constraints of the translated cells (a nominee stays above zero and above the non-nominees of its row, a non-nominee stays below the weakest nominee and, while the row has room, below zero, and the ranks of "frn" rows stay in order). It is drawn exactly from the prior of the level cut to the interval those constraints leave: there is no proposal and nothing to tune. With an intercept the levels are centred and the translation is compensated by the other levels and the intercept, with the prior of the intercept entering: the coefficient prior of a static intercept or, in a dynamic_beta fit of kind "ar1" or "rw1" on the unit period grid, the prior of the intercept's path, which the translation moves by one constant (a static intercept in a dynamic_beta fit enters through its own prior). Hidden cells are labelled by their latent values, as in the sampler, and keep their labels during the move. Panels with absent actors and bipartite fits are covered, and so are dynamic_ab fits, whose sender and receiver translations move the level together with its whole path (the deviations from the level are untouched), and dynamic_beta_per_actor fits, whose actor-specific slopes are a function of their own parameters and the design alone and so stay where they are while the levels, the intercept and the latent array move. The sender translation of a dynamic_ab fit, which a static fit has always made every sweep, runs under the same switch and schedule as the others. Symmetric "cbin" and "frn" fits are not available. The update runs every sweep (the compiled sweep adds roughly a tenth to the time of a sweep); prior$actor_move_every changes that, prior$actor_move = FALSE omits the update, and fit$actor_move records its work.

Two more updates serve the same fits. A row at its cap is bounded below only, but a row with room (fewer nominations than its cap) is pinned from both sides, its non-nominations below zero and its nominations above, and a sparse panel has a few of them (3 to 15 percent of the rows): translating the whole latent array together with the intercept has room for a step of the order of 0.01, so the intercept moved by about \(1/\sqrt{m}\) per sweep however wide its posterior was (4 to 12 effective draws of 1,200 at 170 actors, and a level of the predictor that failed the convergence gate). The level update translates the rows that are free above (the rows at their cap in every period) by one amount and leaves the pinned rows where they are: the intercept takes the compensation (with centred levels it and the pinned rows' levels take it between them), every residual is unchanged, and the amount is drawn exactly from the prior of the levels and the intercept cut at the weakest nomination of the moving rows. It needs an intercept (a static coefficient, or the path of a dynamic_beta fit of kind "ar1" or "rw1" on the unit period grid) and the row effects, since the row effects are what keeps the rows with room in place while the other rows rise (with rvar = FALSE the receiver and reciprocity updates still run); a bipartite fit of ame() (levels free of centring) also draws, exactly, along the ridge the intercept shares with the means of its levels. The dyadic correlation of a directed fit with dcor = TRUE has the same trouble on a larger scale: the non-nominations of rows at their cap only have to stay below their row's weakest nomination, so their pair correlation is whatever \(\rho\) and the latent draws make it, and given the latent array \(\rho\) moves by about \(1/\sqrt{m}\) per sweep, \(m\) the number of dyads, against a posterior a few tenths wide (4 to 8 effective draws of 1,200 at 170 actors). Every tenth visit the reciprocity update integrates the non-nominations and the cells no nomination can sit in out of the density of \(\rho\), draws it by Metropolis steps given the nominations, and redraws the cells it integrated out from their conditionals given the nominations and the new value (prior$actor_move_rho = FALSE omits it; fit$actor_move records its proposals and accepts).

In a dynamic_beta fit of kind "ar1" or "rw1" on the unit period grid with a dynamic intercept, two more updates move the path of the intercept period by period. A period in which almost every row is at its cap (0 and 1 rows with room of 170 in two of four periods of the simulated panels) has a level the data hardly inform, and the level update above, which moves one amount for every period, is stopped by the rows with room of the other periods: the intercepts of those periods had 4 to 7 effective draws of 1,600 (two chains of 800), the least mobile rows with room 13 to 24, and the innovation scale of the path, which follows its shape, 6 to 16; the two-seed convergence gate failed on it (split R-hat 1.10 for "cbin", 1.27 for "frn"). The period update translates the periods that no row with room ties to another one (the connected components of the graph of periods and rows with room) by one amount each, the rows with room compensated by their own levels and the intercepts of the other periods, and draws the amounts exactly. The room update moves the intercept of a period that has rows with room by itself. A row with room is a probit row (its nominations above zero, its non-nominations below), so the Gaussian conditional of the intercept given the latent cells of those rows is narrower than its posterior by the information a latent cell loses when it is integrated out (0.13 to 0.37 per non-nomination). Given a shift of the intercept of a period, the latent slice of the period translates with it, the non-nominations of its rows with room are integrated out of the density of the shift and redrawn from their conditional afterwards, the dyadic correlation entering through the partner cell; the shift is a Metropolis step on that density, so that the intercept moves by its posterior width, not by the width of the Gaussian conditional. A period with a row whose hidden cells leave its room open (fewer observed nominations than the cap and an observed non-nomination) is left to the exact translation. prior$actor_move_period = FALSE and prior$actor_move_room = FALSE omit the two updates (prior$actor_move = FALSE omits every nomination update); fit$actor_move records their work.

Directed binary panels with rank-two Gaussian AR(1) position paths, dynamic additive effects, static coefficients, an intercept, both actor margins and the default unit period grid also receive joint Hamiltonian updates. These integrate both binary latent responses out and retain the full reciprocal-pair likelihood. Factor persistence and stationary scale move in the same Hamiltonian trajectory as their whitened paths, with their original priors and transformation Jacobians retained. The metric uses fixed prior references rather than either proposed endpoint. Additional updates move persistence with path scales, translate factors while integrating and redrawing actor levels, and update dyadic correlation with the latent responses integrated out. Hamiltonian step sizes adapt during burn-in only and survive checkpoints. Set prior$marginal_move = FALSE to disable this group. Other configurations retain their existing updates. These moves preserve the posterior target.

A directed unipartite dynamic_uv fit of the "ar1" or "t" kind with a normal, Poisson or binary outcome starts its chain from a dynamic AR(1) ALS fit of the same model, mapped through als_start_vals, unless start_vals is supplied or prior$als_start = FALSE. Bipartite fits keep the cold start: a bipartite ALS solution parks its scale in the interaction matrix. An ALS start places the initial path on the observed temporal structure; the chain then samples the paths and hyperparameters from there. The ALS fit is deterministic, so the start does not depend on seed; it is an internal penalised point estimate, not the empirical-Bayes fit that method = "als" returns. A start fit that is refused as unconverged (class "lame_als_convergence") contributes its last iterate; a start with non-finite values, or positions beyond prior$uv_max_abs, is not used. fit$als_start records whether it was used.

Dynamic fast fits

A normal, binary or Poisson fit with method = "als" and dynamic_ab, dynamic_beta or dynamic_uv (of the "ar1" or "t" kind, with static or moving latent positions) is fitted by the dynamic empirical-Bayes estimator of the model lame() samples: the actor levels and zero-mean AR(1) deviation paths are random effects and the coefficients have a Gaussian prior; the variance of the cell-level noise (normal and Poisson) and the covariance of the actor levels are estimated by EM under the lame() hyperpriors; the persistence and innovation scale of the additive paths (fit$rho_ab, fit$sigma_ab), the persistences of the moving coefficients (fit$rho_beta) and the persistence and innovation scale of moving positions (fit$rho_uv, fit$sigma_uv) are set by EM too, as smoothing settings chosen by the fit rather than estimates: prediction, simulation and warm starts read them, summary() does not report them, and the sampler estimates the persistence with an interval; the innovation scales of moving coefficients (fit$sigma_beta) are estimated by EM with standard errors; the coefficients have Laplace standard errors (vcov(), confint(), fit$eb$se, fit$eb$se_path for moving coefficients; exact for a normal response); the additive effects, their paths and levels have posterior standard deviations (fit$a_sd, fit$b_sd, fit$a_dynamic_sd, fit$b_dynamic_sd, fit$a_level_sd, fit$b_level_sd), the variance components and the innovation scales of the moving coefficients standard errors by Louis' identity (fit$eb$vc_se, fit$eb$hyper_se), and the cells of the latent product posterior standard deviations (fit$UVPM_sd); summary() shows them with 95 percent intervals. A binary fit with static factors whose signal does not reproduce a static intercept fits the intercept as an rw1 path (fit$eb$intercept_path). A static product is reported at mean zero, its grand mean (and its variance) carried by the intercept; a product below the information threshold is reported with its cell errors (fit$eb$product_weak); a fit whose equations are certified when the passes run out is returned (fit$eb$iteration_limit); static factors are the variational posterior of ame_als() (options(lame.eb_scale) selects the rule that sets the scale of their prior, "cavity" by default) and moving positions have a mean-field Gaussian posterior whose product uncertainty is carried through the cell likelihood; and a directed panel gets the dyadic correlation (dcor).

A normal response has an exact Gaussian cell: the posterior of the coefficients, the levels and the paths at the hyperparameters is exact, the standard errors are the marginal ones given the hyperparameters, the dyadic correlation is an exact bivariate normal pair, and the reported intercept is the level of the effects centred over the actors in each period, as in the samplers. A Poisson response is the Poisson-lognormal model: the correlation of a directed panel is taken at the fitted state, with the information of the pairs in the standard errors; the paths and levels are reported at their first-order posterior mean, the linear predictor (EZ) and the intercept are on the latent scale, and fitted() and predict() return exp(EZ + ve / 2).

A dynamic fit that did not meet its convergence criterion, or whose moving positions have no identified scale, is not returned: the call stops with an error of class "lame_als_convergence", "lame_dynamic_uv_scale_edge" or "lame_dynamic_uv_scale_unsettled" whose field fit holds the last iterate.

See also

ame for cross-sectional models, lame_als for the fast MCMC-free empirical-Bayes fit, als_dynamic_beta for a regression-only penalised smoother on the time-varying coefficient path, lame_resume for resuming saved checkpoints, gof for post-hoc goodness-of-fit computation, gof_plot for visualizing GOF results, latent_positions for extracting latent positions as a tidy data frame, procrustes_align for Procrustes alignment of latent positions, summary.lame for model summaries, coef.lame for coefficient extraction. Long-format edgelists and covariates can be prepared with netify::netify() and passed directly to lame(), or converted explicitly with netify::to_lame(lame = TRUE).

Author

Cassy Dorff, Shahryar Minhas, Tosin Salau

Examples


data(YX_bin_list)
# chains = 1 keeps the example short; the default runs two chains and compares them
fit<-lame(lapply(YX_bin_list$Y, function(y) 1 * (y > 0)), YX_bin_list$X,
          burn=5, nscan=5, odens=1, family="binary", chains = 1)
# you should run the Markov chain much longer than this

# \donttest{
## Time-varying regression coefficients (dynamic_beta).
## Make every dyadic coefficient evolve as an AR(1):
fit_dyn <- lame(lapply(YX_bin_list$Y, function(y) 1 * (y > 0)), YX_bin_list$X,
                family = "binary", R = 0,
                nscan = 60, burn = 15, odens = 5,
                dynamic_beta = "dyad", chains = 1)
dim(fit_dyn$BETA)        # [n_stored, p, T] -- 3-D when dynamic
#> [1] 12  4  4
coef(fit_dyn)            # [p, T] posterior-mean coefficient paths
#>                  t1        t2        t3        t4
#> intercept 0.1239025 0.1239025 0.1239025 0.1239025
#> X1_dyad   0.7232877 0.7160167 0.7483158 0.7566760
#> X2_dyad   0.8777629 0.8917341 0.9069575 0.9131322
#> X3_dyad   1.0828255 1.1037956 1.1561044 1.1344702
confint(fit_dyn)         # per-period 95% credible intervals
#>                     2.5%     97.5%
#> intercept[t1] 0.09131403 0.1517084
#> X1_dyad[t1]   0.67048098 0.7755886
